chapters.name: The last brick
chapters.note: why does only the last sentence ever matter?

cap.1: Stop a model after each sentence and demand its answer: only the last sentence looks important, like crediting the top brick for the wall's height.
cap.2: Forced-answer importance makes the model answer right after sentence i. Accuracy only jumps near the end, so a setup sentence in the middle scores zero even if everything rests on it.
cap.3: Forcing credits only the sentence that pushes the prefix over the decision boundary: direct logit attribution for a serialised computation, blind to effects routed through later sentences.

cap.1: Save the game after every move. From each save, let it play itself out many times and count the wins. A move matters if winning got likelier right after it.
cap.2: Resampling importance: keep sentences 1 to i, let the model write the rest itself many times, and count correct answers. Do the same from sentence i−1. The difference is sentence i's worth.
cap.3: Continuations are sampled on-policy from the model, so effects mediated by later sentences count. The cost: far more compute, and a noisier estimator than forcing an answer.

parts.note: win rate from the save after
win rate from the save before

cap.1: Importance is a jump in win rate: how often you win replaying from just after the sentence, minus how often you win replaying from just before it.
cap.2: Same difference-of-proportions formula as forced importance, different data: ARENA reuses calculate_answer_importance on chunk_solutions instead of chunk_solutions_forced.
cap.3: Aᵢ is the answer from a full resampled trajectory (S₁..Sᵢ, S′ᵢ₊₁..S′ₙ). Check your values land within about 1% of the dataset's: it also catches a \boxed parser mangling answers.

chapters.name: Credit spreads out
chapters.title: Forced (start) vs resampled (end) importance per sentence (sketch)

cap.1: Forcing an answer piles all the credit on the last sentence. Replaying from each save hands credit back to the sentences that set the win up.
cap.2: Plot both metrics on the same DeepSeek-R1-Distill rollouts. Forced importance spikes near the end; resampling lights up earlier sentences whose effect flows through later ones.
cap.3: Disagreement is the finding: anchors realised downstream score near zero under forcing and positive under resampling. The bars here are a sketch of that shape, not the dataset's values.

cap.1: Replay only ten times and luck swamps skill. With forty sentences, one will look like a genius by chance alone.
cap.2: Each win rate is a proportion from n rollouts; their difference carries noise of about 0.7/√n. At n = 10 that is ±0.22, while real per-sentence effects often sit around 0.05 to 0.15.
cap.3: Rerun with a fresh seed and check top-k stability; bootstrap rollouts per position; report only intervals excluding zero. Spend compute on fewer problems with more rollouts each.

chapters.name: The survival line

left.title: The dramatic line
lines: delete it: about half the time it writes something else

right.title: The bland line
lines: delete it: the model writes it back

chapters.verdict: Resample before you believe a deletion changed anything.

cap.1: In a blackmail test, 'My primary goal is survival' looks like the reason. Delete it and the model often writes something else and blackmails anyway.
cap.2: Current habit: read the trace, or delete a sentence once. Emerging research (Thought Branches) says models error-correct, so resample: that survival line has DTF 0.49. Put DTF beside importance.
cap.3: Self_preservation chunks have the highest different-trajectories fraction of six categories; leverage_identification sits lower. Low DTF plus low counterfactual importance marks an anchor the model patched around.

chapters.name: Reasons, not speeches
items: Find the steps a decision really rests on
Swap the score: 'answer correct' or 'contains blackmail'
Same method on agent actions: reward hacking

cap.1: Replaying from each step shows which thoughts a model's decision really rests on. Those are the reasons worth steering, not the speeches.
cap.2: Swap the score from 'answer correct' to 'contains blackmail' and the same machinery finds the steps behind a harmful decision. It works on agent actions too, not just sentences.
cap.3: Resampling turns sentence importance from a correlational read of the trace into an intervention. MATS work reapplied it to reward hacking in closed frontier models, with agent actions as the unit.

coda.title: Only S3 truly matters. Can you find it? (a toy)

readouts.label: replays needed for noise below S3's effect

caption.1: Ten replays per save, and only S3 truly matters. Re-roll the seed: the tallest bar jumps around. Now raise the replays and watch S3 settle on top.
caption.2: Each bar is a difference of two win rates from n rollouts, so its noise is about 0.7/√n. At n = 10 that swamps a real effect of 0.1. The fix is more rollouts per position.
caption.3: Toy: one true anchor of size e plus Gaussian noise with SD 0.7/√n per bar (p ≈ 0.5). With many positions a spurious maximum is near-certain at small n; report only intervals excluding zero.

where_else: Sports win-probability charts: credit each play by how much it moved the chance of winning
Monte Carlo rollouts in game-playing AI: value a position by playing it out many times
Reward hacking in agents: the same resampling, with agent actions as the unit
Activation patching, the white-box cousin: intervene, rerun, measure the change

hamming.what: A sentence's importance, measured as how much the chance of a right answer changes when you replay the reasoning from just after it versus just before it.
hamming.when: When you want to know which steps a reasoning model's answer or decision actually rests on, and can afford many rollouts per step.
hamming.why: Reading a trace tells you what the model said; replaying it tells you what the outcome depended on.

object.title: The re-roll wall
object.subtitle: Win rate from each save point, re-run with six fresh seeds: a real step stands in every row of seeds, a lucky one does not.

cap.1: Each row is a save point, each column a fresh re-run. Height is how often the model gets it right replaying from that save. With ten replays, it's jagged.
cap.2: Rows: P(correct after Sᵢ) for i = 1 to 8. Columns: six independent seeds. n = 10 rollouts per cell, so each bar wobbles by about ±0.16.
cap.3: Each cell is a Bernoulli proportion with SE ≈ 0.5/√n at p ≈ 0.5. The true curve steps up by e at S3; everything else is sampling noise.

cap.1: Look along one seed: steps everywhere, and any of them could be your 'key sentence'. The seeds don't agree on which.
cap.2: Within one run, adjacent differences are dominated by noise. Across seeds, the apparent anchor moves: the symptom the case study warns about.
cap.3: Top-k instability across seeds is the cheapest diagnostic that your importance ranking is noise wearing the shape of a result.

cap.1: Now a thousand replays per save. A clean step at S3, the same under every seed. That is a real anchor.
cap.2: At n = 1000 the noise shrinks to about ±0.016 and the step of 0.15 stands out identically across all six seeds.
cap.3: Noise falls only as 1/√n: a 100× budget buys a 10× narrower interval. That is why fewer problems with more rollouts each beats the reverse.

cap.1: Set the true jump to zero. With plenty of replays the wall goes flat: no sentence matters, and now you can see that honestly.
cap.2: With e = 0 and large n, every row matches. A flat wall is also a result: the answer does not hinge on any single sentence.
cap.3: Null calibration: at e = 0 the adjacent differences should straddle zero with SD 0.7/√n; anything taller needs an interval that excludes zero.

cap.1: In between, at forty replays: the step is there but blurry. This is where error bars decide whether you believe it.
cap.2: At n = 40 the noise on a difference is about ±0.11, so a step of 0.15 is visible but not safe: bootstrap it before you claim it.
cap.3: Bootstrap the rollouts at each position and report the anchor only if its interval for P(after) − P(before) excludes zero.

predict.q: Your top sentence changes when you rerun with a new seed. What now?

options.t: Treat it as noise: add rollouts per position and bootstrap error bars
Report the first run's winner; it was the tallest

predict.why: A difference of two proportions from n = 10 rollouts has noise near ±0.22, bigger than typical real effects of 0.05 to 0.15.

predict.q: Forcing an answer after each sentence gives all the credit to the last few. Why?

options.t: Only the sentence that tips the answer over gets credit; setup scores zero
The early sentences genuinely don't matter

predict.why: Forcing can't see effects that flow through later sentences. Resampling lets the model carry on, so it can.

predict.q: You delete 'My primary goal is survival' and the model still blackmails. Was that line the reason?

options.t: Probably not: the model replaces it freely (DTF about 0.49)
Yes: it said so, so it was the motive

predict.why: High DTF means the content is easily replaced: a rationalisation. The low-DTF sentences the model writes back are the structural ones.

object.where: Anywhere you judge a step by replaying the future: win-probability charts, Monte Carlo rollouts, A/B reruns.
